steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a SIFT-aided rectified 2D-DIC method for measuring displacement and strain in asphalt concrete tests. Cover why 2D-DIC is used, what it requires, the problem of a non-perpendicular camera, existing fixes, and what our method offers.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. DIC in asphalt concrete testing; 2D-DIC vs. stereo-DIC
2. Advantages of 2D-DIC
3. Requirements for accurate 2D-DIC; perpendicularity hard to meet in AC labs
4. Existing methods for non-perpendicularity
5. Our method: no additional equipment

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. DIC
- optical displacement and strain measurement technique
- vital tool in AC: material properties, test protocols, theoretical models
- most popular: 2D-DIC and stereo-DIC
- 2D-DIC: single fixed camera, in-plane displacement of nominal planar objects; not applicable for non-planar surface or non-negligible out-of-plane displacement
- stereo-DIC: two synchronized cameras, 3D displacement, binocular stereo-vision principle

2. Advantages of 2D-DIC
- simple setup: single charge-coupled device (CCD) camera vs. two synchronized cameras
- simple algorithm: correlation between deformed images and reference image
- stereo-DIC: stereo-calibration, stereo matching (cross-camera), temporal matching, triangulation -> more uncertainty from algorithm choices in each step, impacts precision

3. Requirements
- planar specimen surface
- small out-of-plane deformation
- no geometric distortion in imaging system
- sensor parallel to specimen surface (principal axis perpendicular)
- first three easy in AC lab tests; last one often hard due to equipment
- Fig. 1: only one of three I-FIT testing devices has open space for perpendicularity

4. Existing methods (past decade), two groups
- modify experimental setup / transform images
- imaging system change: bilateral telecentric lens, sensitive to in-plane, insensitive to out-of-plane displacement
- non-deformable compensation specimen attached to testing surface, moves rigidly; parametric model fitted to its displacement field corrects error
- rectification of images from non-perpendicular camera: standard camera calibration with regular grid pattern; extrinsic and intrinsic parameters; DIC on rectified images

5. Our method
- existing fixes need extra equipment (special lens, compensation specimen, grid pattern) -> simplicity of 2D-DIC compromised
- simple, reliable, no additional equipment
- validated numerically (synthetic images) and experimentally (I-FIT)
- pre-processing for CrackPropNet: crack propagation on I-FIT specimen surface

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Digital image correlation (DIC) is a technique for measuring displacement and strain optically. Since it was introduced for asphalt concrete (AC), DIC has become a vital tool for evaluating AC material properties, validating test protocols, and verifying theoretical models. The most popular DIC algorithms are two-dimensional (2D)-DIC and stereo-DIC. 2D-DIC uses one fixed camera to measure the in-plane displacement of objects that are nominally planar. But the 2D-DIC method cannot be used when the surface of the test specimen is not planar, or when the out-of-plane displacement cannot be neglected. Stereo-DIC, which uses two synchronized cameras, was proposed to measure 3D displacement based on the binocular stereo-vision principle.

2D-DIC is still one of the most popular optical technologies, because it has the following advantages:

- 1. Simple experimental setup: 2D-DIC needs only one charge-coupled device (CCD) camera. Stereo-DIC needs two synchronized cameras.

- 2. Simple algorithm: In 2D-DIC, computing the displacement field only relies on the correlation between deformed images taken after deformation and a reference image taken before deformation. Stereo-DIC needs a complicated procedure that includes stereo-calibration of the two-camera unit, stereo matching (i.e., cross-camera matching), temporal matching, and triangulation to reconstruct 3D coordinates. So stereo-DIC has more uncertainty because of the different algorithms chosen in each step, and this impacts the final precision of the measurements.

But an accurate 2-D DIC measurement is only possible when the following requirements are met:

- 1. Specimen surface is planar.

- 2. Out-of-plane deformation of the specimen is small enough.

- 3. Imaging system does not suffer from geometric distortion.

- 4. Charged-couple device sensor is parallel to the specimen surface (i.e., the camera's principal axis is perpendicular to the specimen surface).

The first three requirements are easy to satisfy in most AC laboratory tests. The last one, however, is often hard to meet because of equipment limitations. For example, as Fig. 1 shows, only one of the three testing devices for the Illinois-flexibility index test (I-FIT) has open space so that the perpendicularity requirement can be satisfied.

- past decade: a few methods to alleviate effect of non-perpendicularity; two groups by fundamental principle
- group 1: modify experimental setup or transform images
  - changes to imaging system: bilateral telecentric lens (sensitive to in-plane, insensitive to out-of-plane displacement)
  - non-deformable compensation specimen attached to testing surface, moves rigidly during loading; parametric model fitted to its displacement field corrects error
- group 2: rectification of images from non-perpendicular camera
  - standard camera calibration with regular grid pattern; extrinsic + intrinsic parameters used for rectification; DIC on rectified images
- problem: extra equipment (special lens, compensation specimen, grid pattern) compromises simplicity of 2D-DIC
- our method: simple, reliable, no additional equipment; validated numerically (synthetic images) and experimentally (I-FIT); pre-processing for CrackPropNet crack propagation on I-FIT specimen surface

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Digital image correlation (DIC) is a technique for measuring displacement and strain optically. Since it was introduced for asphalt concrete (AC), DIC has become a vital tool for evaluating AC material properties, validating test protocols, and verifying theoretical models. The most popular DIC algorithms are two-dimensional (2D)-DIC and stereo-DIC. 2D-DIC uses one fixed camera to measure the in-plane displacement of objects that are nominally planar. But the 2D-DIC method cannot be used when the surface of the test specimen is not planar, or when the out-of-plane displacement cannot be neglected. Stereo-DIC, which uses two synchronized cameras, was proposed to measure 3D displacement based on the binocular stereo-vision principle.

2D-DIC is still one of the most popular optical technologies, because it has the following advantages:

- 1. Simple experimental setup: 2D-DIC needs only one charge-coupled device (CCD) camera. Stereo-DIC needs two synchronized cameras.

- 2. Simple algorithm: In 2D-DIC, computing the displacement field only relies on the correlation between deformed images taken after deformation and a reference image taken before deformation. Stereo-DIC needs a complicated procedure that includes stereo-calibration of the two-camera unit, stereo matching (i.e., cross-camera matching), temporal matching, and triangulation to reconstruct 3D coordinates. So stereo-DIC has more uncertainty because of the different algorithms chosen in each step, and this impacts the final precision of the measurements.

But an accurate 2-D DIC measurement is only possible when the following requirements are met:

- 1. Specimen surface is planar.

- 2. Out-of-plane deformation of the specimen is small enough.

- 3. Imaging system does not suffer from geometric distortion.

- 4. Charged-couple device sensor is parallel to the specimen surface (i.e., the camera's principal axis is perpendicular to the specimen surface).

The first three requirements are easy to satisfy in most AC laboratory tests. The last one, however, is often hard to meet because of equipment limitations. For example, as Fig. 1 shows, only one of the three testing devices for the Illinois-flexibility index test (I-FIT) has open space so that the perpendicularity requirement can be satisfied.

In the past decade, researchers have proposed a few methods to reduce the effect of non-perpendicularity on 2D-DIC. Based on their fundamental principles they can be put into two groups. The first group modifies the experimental setup or transforms images. For example, one study proposed changes to the imaging system, recommending a bilateral telecentric lens because it is relatively highly sensitive to in-plane displacement and insensitive to out-of-plane displacement. Another study suggested attaching a non-deformable compensation specimen to the testing surface. The compensation specimen moves rigidly with the testing specimen during loading, and the measurement error can be corrected with a parametric model fitted using the displacement field of the compensation specimen. The second group applies rectification to transform images that were collected with a non-perpendicular camera setting. Here the standard camera calibration procedure was followed with a regular grid pattern, and the extrinsic and intrinsic parameters of the camera were determined and used for the rectification. DIC analysis was then done on the rectified images, which can be collected under a perpendicular camera setting.

These approaches correct the errors caused by non-perpendicularity effectively, but they need additional equipment, such as a special lens, a compensation specimen, or a grid pattern, and so the simplicity of 2D-DIC is compromised. To get the full benefits of 2D-DIC, this paper proposes a method that is simple and reliable and does not need any additional equipment. We validated the proposed method numerically with synthetic images and experimentally in an I-FIT. Also, we applied the proposed method as a pre-processing technique to help CrackPropNet measure crack propagation on the surface of an I-FIT specimen.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Digital image correlation (DIC) is an optical displacement and strain measurement technique. Since its introduction for asphalt concrete (AC) applications, DIC has become a vital tool in evaluating AC material properties, validating test protocols, and verifying theoretical models [1,2,3,4,5]. The most popular DIC algorithms include two-dimensional (2D)-DIC and stereo-DIC. 2D-DIC uses a single fixed camera to measure the in-plane displacement of nominal planar objects. However, the 2D-DIC method is not applicable when the test specimen surface is non-planar or the out-of-plane displacement is non-negligible. The stereo-DIC method, on the other hand, which uses two synchronized cameras, was proposed to measure 3D displacement based on the binocular stereo-vision principle [6].

2D-DIC remains one of the most popular optical technologies because of the following advantages:

- 1. Simple experimental setup: For 2D-DIC, only a single charge-coupled device (CCD) camera is needed, whereas stereo-DIC requires two synchronized cameras [7].

- 2. Simple algorithm: The computation of the displacement field in 2D-DIC relies solely on the correlation between deformed images captured after deformation and a reference image captured before deformation. Stereo-DIC, on the other hand, entails a complex procedure that includes stereo-calibration of the two-camera unit, stereo matching (i.e., cross-camera matching), temporal matching, and triangulation for reconstructing 3D coordinates [8]. Hence, stereo-DIC has more uncertainty due to the different algorithms chosen in each step, which impacts the ultimate precision of measurements [9,10].

However, an accurate 2-D DIC measurement can only be achieved when the following requirements are met [11]:

- 1. Specimen surface is planar.

- 2. Out-of-plane deformation of the specimen is small enough.

- 3. Imaging system does not suffer from geometric distortion.

- 4. Charged-couple device sensor is parallel to the specimen surface (i.e., the camera's principal axis is perpendicular to the specimen surface).

The first three requirements can easily be satisfied in most AC laboratory tests, but equipment limitations often make the last one difficult to meet. For example, as shown in Fig. 1, only one of the three testing devices for the Illinois-flexibility index test (I-FIT) offers open space to satisfy the perpendicularity requirement [12].

In the past decade, researchers have proposed a few methods to alleviate the effect of non-perpendicularity on 2D-DIC, which can be categorized into two groups based on their fundamental principles. The first modifies the experimental setup or transforms images. For example, \citeN pan2013high proposed changes to the imaging system, recommending a bilateral telecentric lens for its relatively high sensitivity to in-plane displacement and insensitivity to out-of-plane displacement. Moreover, \citeN pan2013high1 suggested attaching a non-deformable compensation specimen onto the testing surface. During loading, the compensation specimen moves rigidly with the testing specimen, and the measurement error can be corrected by applying a parametric model fitted using the compensation specimen's displacement field. The second group applies rectification to transform images collected under a non-perpendicular camera setting [13]. The standard camera calibration procedure was followed using a regular grid pattern, and the camera's extrinsic and intrinsic parameters were determined and used to conduct the rectification. DIC analysis was then conducted on the rectified images, which can be collected under a perpendicular camera setting.

While these approaches effectively correct errors caused by non-perpendicularity, the simplicity of 2D-DIC is compromised by the need for additional equipment, such as a special lens, compensation specimen, or grid pattern. To fully leverage the benefits of 2D-DIC, this paper proposes a simple and reliable method that needs no additional equipment. The proposed method was validated numerically using synthetic images and experimentally in an I-FIT. In addition, as a pre-processing technique, the proposed method was applied to assist CrackPropNet in measuring crack propagation on an I-FIT specimen surface.
